title: Invoice fraud and the changed account number
body_md:
## A true invoice, a false destination

The invoice lands in the same email thread as every one before it: same logo, same amount, same friendly sign-off. Then a short reply: the supplier has moved banks, please pay the account below.

That is business email compromise. Sometimes the sender address is a careful imitation. Sometimes it is the supplier’s real mailbox in someone else’s hands, and then the name, signature, domain and even the old thread all look right, because they are right. The attacker reads along and sends a routine-looking change of bank details to catch the next payment. An IBAN that passes validation proves only that the number is built correctly, not whose account it is. The rule that holds up is to verify the **change** through a channel you trusted before it arrived.

### Check the change, not the sender

Before you touch the vendor record, compare the invoice with the original contract and the approved payee. Then phone a number already stored in the supplier record, never the one in the new email or its attachment, and ask your known contact to confirm the legal payee and the new details under your organization’s usual procedure. If you have no reliable number, take the question to the person who onboarded the supplier. A number from a search result will not do. Write down who verified, when, and what they confirmed. A second approver should see the history of the account change, not just the same forwarded email.

### Honest suppliers change banks too

Suppliers really do switch banks, and confirming it is no accusation. The callback has a weak spot of its own: if an attacker has already swapped the stored number, you will be confirming the fraud with the fraudster. So protect the supplier master record, and call a contact you validated earlier. A payment deadline is a reason to escalate, not to skip the check.

If the money has already gone, call the bank it left from right away and ask for a recall or reversal. Tell finance and security, keep the original message and the payment record, and report through your local channels. The FBI’s IC3 complaint and bank-recall details are US-specific. A recall is a request, and nobody can promise it will work.

widget_config.goal: Verify a changed payment instruction without trusting the thread it arrived in.
widget_config.today_action: Find your organization’s approved vendor contact record and its procedure for payment changes. If either is missing, ask the owner to set it up before the next changed invoice arrives.
widget_config.scope: The organizational control applies anywhere. The FBI IC3 reporting and the bank-recall description concern US banking, and bank procedures and liability differ elsewhere. The suppliers and cases are invented. Checked 2026-10-20.

sources.title: FBI IC3: Business Email Compromise
sources.scope: The US complaint and recall route. Confirming through another channel is sound practice anywhere.

sources.title: FBI IC3: Complaint FAQ
sources.scope: How US complaints are filed and what evidence to keep. IC3 does not accept attachments.

blocks.title: The right supplier, the wrong account
blocks.situation: An agency’s invoice turns up inside an existing email thread, with the usual logo and the usual amount. A later reply changes one thing, the beneficiary account, and blames a bank migration.
blocks.analysis: A thread that looks continuous does not prove the mailbox is in the right hands. Freeze the change of payee, phone the supplier contact you verified before, and log what they say under the company procedure. If that contact cannot confirm it, escalate before anything is paid.

blocks.title: A bank move that was announced
blocks.situation: At the last meeting the vendor told procurement that its account would change. The formal notice now arrives by email. Procurement phones its known finance contact, and the organization updates its master record with two approvers signing off.
blocks.analysis: A bank change is not fraud in itself. Confirmation through another channel and a protected change record settle the doubt. Keep the original invoice and the approval trail, and do not ask suppliers to promise they will never change their details.

blocks.title: Same thread, new account
blocks.setup: An invented scenario. You are processing an invoice from Blue Harbor Studio, and payment is due soon. In a thread you recognize, a reply gives a new account to pay into.

steps.prompt: A reply in a familiar thread supplies a new account. What do you treat as unverified?

choices.text: The new beneficiary, however familiar the invoice and the thread look.
choices.consequence: The payment waits on the one detail nobody has verified, the new account.
choices.explanation: A real mailbox that has been taken over can carry the instruction too.

choices.consequence: Whoever controls a mailbox on that domain could have sent it.
choices.explanation: A matching domain alone does not validate changed bank details.

steps.prompt: The email also gives a new finance phone number. Whom do you call?

choices.text: The number in the change notice.
choices.consequence: An accomplice picks up and confirms the false account.
choices.explanation: That channel belongs to the message you are trying to check.

choices.text: The number saved before this request, asking the contact you already know.
choices.consequence: The check runs on a different line from the request.
choices.explanation: A request must never supply its own verifier.

steps.prompt: You phone the number saved before this email, and nobody answers. The bank change is still unconfirmed and payment is due today. What next?

choices.text: Take it to whoever owns the supplier relationship in your organization, and hold the account change until it is confirmed.
choices.consequence: The deadline stays in view, and the control stays in place.
choices.explanation: An exception to the process belongs to someone authorized to approve it.

choices.text: Pay the new account so the invoice is not late.
choices.consequence: The money goes to a recipient who may be false.
choices.explanation: A due date says when to pay. It says nothing about who owns the account.

steps.prompt: A separate situation: a colleague has already paid into the changed account. What comes first?

choices.text: Wait for the supplier to notice that nothing arrived.
choices.consequence: The window for a possible recall closes.
choices.explanation: Waiting shrinks the bank’s chance of getting a recall request through.

choices.text: Contact the bank the money left from, alert finance and security, and keep the records.
choices.consequence: The bank can look at recall options while the company limits further loss.
choices.explanation: Speed helps, but reversal is never guaranteed.

blocks.debrief: A changed destination needs its own callback, even inside a genuine thread. Guard the old contact details and keep the approval trail. Run it again with the other answers and see where each one leaves the money.

questions.prompt: An IBAN passes validation. What has that established?

choices.text: That the named supplier owns it.
choices.explanation: Ownership has to be confirmed separately.

choices.text: Only that the number is built correctly, not whose account it is.
choices.explanation: A format check cannot tell you who the intended beneficiary is.

questions.prompt: The supplier really has changed banks. Is the callback still worth making?

choices.text: No. A callback accuses an honest supplier.
choices.explanation: Verification is routine. It is not an accusation.

choices.text: Yes. It confirms the genuine change without blocking it.
choices.explanation: A good control handles real changes as well as fraudulent ones.

questions.prompt: The payment has already left. What cannot wait?

choices.text: Asking the sending bank about a recall or reversal, and alerting your internal teams.
choices.explanation: The bank decides which options exist, and your own teams can stop a repeat.

choices.text: Looking harder at the email signature.
choices.explanation: That will not retrieve the money or stop another payment.
